key_works: Boddu–Jain–Kapshikar (2021/2024), [*Quantum secure non-malleable-extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03097); Li (2023), [*Two Source Extractors for Asymptotically Optimal Entropy, and (Many) More*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06802).

title: G11. Explicit seeded condensers with coefficient one on log error
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Match existential lossless-condenser parameters \(d=\log(n-k)+\log(1/\varepsilon)+O(1)\) and \(m=k+d+\log(1/\varepsilon)+O(1)\).
status: Random functions achieve this leading error dependence; general explicit constructions remain weaker.
why: The coefficient of \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) controls several downstream seedless-condensing constructions.
key_works: Goodman–Li–Zuckerman (2024), [*Improved Condensers for Chor-Goldreich Sources*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08142).

title: G12. Constant-factor gap loss for low-entropy Chor–Goldreich sources
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Condense n-bit blocks with at least \(n^{0.99}\) conditional min-entropy each to rate at least 0.9, with deficiency \(O(n-n^{0.99}+\log(1/\varepsilon))\).
status: Explicit low-entropy condensation is established; current constructions can enlarge the inherited deficiency by a polynomial factor.
why: Would prevent repeated weak-source processing from wasting most usable entropy.
key_works: Goodman–Li–Zuckerman (2024), [*Improved Condensers for Chor-Goldreich Sources*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08142).

title: G13. Linear entropy deficiency for unpredictable sources
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Improve online condensation of \((\delta,\rho)\)-unpredictable sources to rate \(1-O(\rho)\), with \(\Omega(\delta dt)\) output and the stipulated polynomial-in-\(\rho\) error.
status: Doron–Moshkovitz–Oh–Zuckerman explicitly conjecture this improvement; their random-walk construction gives rate \(1-\rho^{1/C}\).
why: Would sharply improve the quality of randomness extracted from occasionally predictable blocks.
key_works: Doron–Moshkovitz–Oh–Zuckerman (2025), [*Online Condensing of Unpredictable Sources via Random Walks*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.30).

title: G14. Explicit condensing with constant-size online blocks
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: For sufficiently large constant block length, explicitly condense \(\ell\) online symbol-fixing blocks with at least \(0.51\ell\) uniform good blocks to \(\Omega(\ell)\) bits at rate 0.99 and exponentially small error.
status: Existential constructions achieve this; explicit constructions require growing block length.
why: Would handle many weak contributors producing only short messages.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5).

title: G15. The online bit-fixing non-condensing conjecture
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Resolve whether deterministic condensation can nontrivially raise the entropy rate of online nonoblivious bit-fixing sources in the constant-rate regime, allowing small smoothing error.
status: Zero-error obstructions are known; the authors explicitly conjecture a remaining non-condensing barrier.
why: Would explain a fundamental difference between one-bit and longer-block contributions.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04115), open-problems section.

title: G16. Exact online-corruption threshold for extraction
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Determine optimal corruption thresholds for constant-error online extraction, separately for one-bit contributions and symbols of length at least \(\log\ell\).
status: Constructions tolerate \(\Omega(\ell/\log\ell)\) corrupt bits or \(\Omega(\ell/\log^*\ell)\) corrupt symbols; known lower bounds leave gaps.
why: Would identify the maximum adversarial participation compatible with shared randomness.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04115); Ben-Or–Linial (1989), [*Collective Coin Flipping*](https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~nati/PAPERS/coll_coin_fl.pdf).

title: G17. Constant entropy deficiency for online symbol sources
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Obtain condensers for uniform \(0.51\)-good-fraction online symbol-fixing sources with \(O(1)\) output entropy deficiency, fixed small error, and growing output.
status: Even existence is explicitly open in the 2026 formulation; available deficiency bounds grow with parameters.
why: Constant deficiency would bring adversarial-source outputs close to ideal random seeds.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5).

title: G18. Seedless samplable condensing beyond black-box assumptions
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Construct seedless condensers for general efficient samplers from established assumptions such as LWE using non-black-box techniques, matching specialized-assumption parameters.
status: Freitag–Silbak–Wichs give near-optimal specialized-hashing constructions and a black-box barrier for standard game-based assumptions.
why: Would give a conventional foundation for deterministic improvement of algorithmically generated randomness.
key_works: Freitag–Silbak–Wichs (2025), [*Seedless Condensers for Efficiently Samplable Sources*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1783).

title: G19. Quasilinear Raz extraction without auxiliary length restrictions
open: Extend quasilinear Raz extraction throughout its original asymmetric source-length regime, removing \(n_2\le n_1/2\) and associated auxiliary-parameter restrictions.
status: The 2025 implementation already runs in \(O(n_1\log^2 n_1)\) on its supported parameters; broadening that range is explicitly open.
why: Would make fast extraction available for more realistic unequal-source configurations.
key_works: Foreman–Wooltorton–Milner–Curchod (2025), [*An efficient construction of Raz’s two-source randomness extractor with improved parameters*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15547).

title: G20. Ordinary-to-seedless-nonmalleable extractor conversion
open: Convert arbitrary two-source or affine extractors into seedless nonmalleable extractors with polynomial error loss, constant-factor entropy overhead, and constant-fraction output.
status: Explicitly asked in 2024. Strong dedicated constructions do not supply a generic conversion.
why: Would allow advances in ordinary extraction to transfer automatically to tamper-resistant randomness.
key_works: Li–Zhong (2024), [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108).

title: G21. Negligible-error two-source nonmalleability at polylogarithmic entropy
open: Extract nonconstant output with error \(n^{-\omega(1)}\) from two polylogarithmic-entropy sources against separate tampering functions, at least one fixed-point-free.
status: The 2024 constructions achieve polynomial error with long output or constant output at logarithmic entropy.
why: Would support negligible-error tamper resistance from extremely weak independent sources.
key_works: Li–Zhong (2024), [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108).

title: G22. High-entropy extraction with seed depending on deficiency
open: For min-entropy \(n-\Delta\), recover almost all entropy with seed \(2\log(1/\varepsilon)+f(\Delta)\), without additional dependence on n.
status: Explicitly identified in 2025. Constant-seed optimal-output constructions for symbol-fixing sources exploit structure absent from arbitrary high-entropy sources.
why: Nearly uniform sources should require randomness proportional to their deficiency.
key_works: Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya (2025), [*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03090).

title: G23. Smaller alphabets for fast nearly-MDS erasure codes
open: Construct explicit rate-R codes correcting \(1-R-\eta\) adversarial erasures with quasilinear encoding and decoding over alphabets approaching \(\exp(O(1/\eta^2))\).
status: The 2025 fast construction has alphabet dependence approximately \(\exp(\widetilde O(1/\eta^4))\); better nonexplicit tradeoffs do not yield the same uniform algorithms.
why: Smaller alphabets improve practical coding and associated extractor constructions.
key_works: Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya (2025), [*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03090).

title: G24. Short-seed linear extractors with linear output
open: Construct strong extractors linear in the source for each fixed seed, with \(d=O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\), \(m=\Omega(k)\), and \(k\ge C\log(n/\varepsilon)\) throughout the low-entropy regime.
status: Known linear constructions trade seed length against output length; unrestricted seeded extraction does not settle this linearity-constrained target.
why: Linearity enables efficient integration with coding, sharing, and algebraic protocols.
key_works: Doron–Fridman (2025), [*Bit-Fixing Extractors for Almost-Logarithmic Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2025.33), Section 2.3.

title: G25. Optimal-order seeded extraction against unrestricted quantum information
open: Extract \(\Omega(k)\) bits with seed \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) whenever \(H_{\min}(X\mid E)\ge k\ge C\log(n/\varepsilon)\), for arbitrary-dimensional quantum E.
status: Trevisan-style constructions recover nearly all entropy with longer seeds; shorter-seed results impose restrictions. The 2016 general-optimality claim was withdrawn.
why: Would match classical-order extraction parameters against unrestricted quantum storage.
key_works: De–Portmann–Vidick–Renner (2012), [*Trevisan’s Extractor in the Presence of Quantum Side Information*](https://doi.org/10.1137/100813683); Ben-Aroya–Ta-Shma (2012), [*Better short-seed quantum-proof extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3737); [withdrawn 2016 claim](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.04194).

title: G26. Negligible-error affine nonmalleability at polylogarithmic entropy
open: Construct polynomial-time affine nonmalleable extractors for \(k=\operatorname{polylog}n\), error \(n^{-\omega(1)}\), and output \(k^{\Omega(1)}\).
status: Polynomial error was achieved in 2024. The October 2026 result gives exponentially small error at constant entropy rate and strong near-\(n/\log n\) results, leaving this low-entropy target open.
why: Would combine very weak algebraic randomness with cryptographic-strength tamper resistance.
key_works: Li–Zhong (2024), [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108); Li–Zhong (2026), [*Non-Malleable Affine Extractors with Small Error and Complexity Lower Bounds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02407).

title: R3-001. Beimel’s exponential secret-sharing conjecture
open: Exhibit an \(n\)-party access structure for which every perfectly private, perfectly reconstructing scheme for a one-bit secret requires total share length \(2^{\Omega(n)}\), allowing arbitrary nonlinear sharing and reconstruction.
status: Conjectured in Beimel’s 1996 thesis. August–September 2026 preprints improve the general bounds to \(\Omega(n^2)\) versus \(2^{0.494n+o(n)}\); exponential lower bounds still require reconstruction restrictions.
why: Determines whether complicated access policies inherently require exponentially large information-theoretic storage.
key_works: Kasper Green Larsen and Mark Simkin (2019), [*Towards an Exponential Lower Bound for Secret Sharing*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/174); Christopher Williamson (2026), [*Secret Sharing at the Shannon Ceiling*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17047); Oded Nir (2026), [*Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/146/revision/1/download), September revision.

title: R3-002. Polynomial shares for slice access structures
open: Determine whether every slice access structure has polynomial total share size for a **one-bit secret**, or exhibit a slice requiring superpolynomial size. A slice is arbitrary on one cardinality layer, rejects smaller sets, and accepts larger sets.
status: One-bit constructions give \(2^{\widetilde O(\sqrt n)}\) shares. Polynomial information ratios for sufficiently long secrets, including September 2026 multislice results, leave this question open.
why: Tests whether a complicated individual layer of an authorization policy admits substantial compression.
key_works: Tianren Liu and Vinod Vaikuntanathan (2018), [*Breaking the Circuit-Size Barrier in Secret Sharing*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/333), DOI:10.1145/3188745.3188936; Benny Applebaum and Oded Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/); Amos Beimel and Oded Nir (2026), [*The Power of Multislices in Monotone Computation*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/213/).

title: R3-003. Efficient information-theoretic sharing for monotone circuits
open: Compile every polynomial-size monotone circuit into a perfectly secure secret-sharing scheme with polynomial-time sharing and reconstruction and polynomial total shares.
status: Monotone formulas admit efficient schemes; general circuits remain unresolved. Near-quadratic separations between circuit size and required shares already rule out very low overhead.
why: Would make information-theoretic access control scale with an efficiently evaluable policy.
key_works: Josh Cohen Benaloh and Jerry Leichter (1988), *Generalized Secret Sharing and Monotone Functions*; Amos Beimel (2023), [*Lower Bounds for Secret-Sharing Schemes for k-Hypergraphs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2023.16); Applebaum–Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/).

title: R3-004. Graph access structures beyond the logarithmic lower bound
open: Determine the worst-case information ratio for graph access structures, where a set reconstructs exactly when it contains an edge. Prove an \(\omega(\log n)\) lower bound on maximum share size relative to secret size, or substantially improve the \(O(n/\log n)\) upper bound.
status: This gap persists in the checked 2020 and 2025 treatments. Stronger lower bounds for linear schemes do not settle unrestricted nonlinear sharing.
why: Isolates a simple authorization rule whose storage complexity remains poorly understood.
key_works: Amos Beimel and Oriol Farràs (2020), [*The Share Size of Secret-Sharing Schemes for Almost All Access Structures and Graphs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/664); László Csirmaz (2009), *An Impossibility Result on Graph Secret Sharing*; Applebaum–Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/).

title: R3-005. The three-uniform hypergraph share-size gap
open: Determine the optimal worst-case total information ratio when minimal authorized sets all have size three. Improve the \(\Omega(n^{3/2})\) lower bound or \(O(n^3/\log n)\) upper bound in the long-secret regime.
status: Beimel’s 2023 lower bound reaches \(n^{3/2}\); decomposition constructions leave a polynomial gap. Large unauthorized sets are allowed, distinguishing this model from slices.
why: Measures how expensive authorization by triples can be.
key_works: Amos Beimel (2023), [*Lower Bounds for Secret-Sharing Schemes for k-Hypergraphs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2023.16), especially the \(k=3\) case.

title: R3-006. Truth-table recognition of extremely cheap secret sharing
open: Given a monotone truth table of size \(N=2^n\), distinguish maximum share size two from \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) in \(\operatorname{poly}(N)\), or even \(N^{O(\log N)}\), time, under the promise that the latter instances exist.
status: Explicitly posed in 2025; existing hardness results leave this coarse promise gap unresolved.
why: Would identify authorization policies admitting unexpectedly small shares.
key_works: Benny Applebaum and Oded Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/), §2.5, Question 1.

title: R3-007. Approximating P4-free covers for linear secret sharing
open: Approximate a bipartite graph’s minimum edge cover by bipartite subgraphs containing no induced four-vertex path, within a constant or mildly growing factor in polynomial time.
status: The 2025 connection characterizes constant-size linear shares using this cover number. Exact computation is NP-hard; the requested approximation remains open.
why: Would turn a structural characterization of cheap sharing into a policy-analysis algorithm.
key_works: Benny Applebaum and Oded Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/), Theorem 2.5 and §2.5, Question 2.

title: R3-008. Duality for perfect nonlinear secret sharing
open: Decide whether an access structure and its dual always have the same optimal maximum-share information ratio under perfect reconstruction and perfect privacy. A concrete unequal pair would refute the conjecture.
status: Equality holds for multilinear constructions. Csirmaz’s 2019/2021 counterexample uses almost-perfect sharing on 174 participants, leaving the perfect model unresolved.
why: Determines whether complementing an authorization policy can change its fundamental storage cost.
key_works: László Csirmaz (2019; journal 2021), [*Secret Sharing and Duality*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13663); Applebaum–Nir (2021), [*Upslices, Downslices, and Secret-Sharing with Complexity of 1.5ⁿ*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2021/052/).

title: R3-009. Exact black-box shares when n is not a power of two
open: For two-out-of-\(n\) sharing over arbitrary finite abelian groups of unknown order, determine the minimum average number of group elements per share when \(n\) is not a power of two.
status: The checked bounds are \(\log_2 n\) below and \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) above. The power-of-two case is optimal; the remaining gap is reposed in 2026.
why: Resolves an integrality gap in threshold group cryptography.
key_works: Ronald Cramer and Serge Fehr (2002), *Optimal Black-Box Secret Sharing over Arbitrary Abelian Groups*; Cramer, Fehr and Martijn Stam (2005), *Black-Box Secret Sharing from Primitive Sets in Algebraic Number Fields*; Milan Boutros, Ignacio Cascudo, Ronald Cramer, Daniël van Gent and Chaoping Xing (2026), [*On Exceptional Cliques in Matrix Rings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24586), §13.

title: R3-010. Amortizing black-box group secret sharing
open: Share \(m\) secrets from a black-box finite abelian group \(G\) with fewer group elements per secret than independent repetition, allowing operations on individual coordinates of \(G^m\).
status: Reposed in 2026. Single-secret lower bounds on \(G^m\) do not cover coordinate access.
why: Could reduce storage for many threshold keys.
key_works: Boutros, Cascudo, Cramer, van Gent and Xing (2026), [*On Exceptional Cliques in Matrix Rings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24586), §13; Ronald Cramer and Chaoping Xing (2020), *Blackbox Secret Sharing Revisited: A Coding-Theoretic Approach with Application to Expansionless Near-Threshold Schemes*.

title: R3-011. Optimal exceptional integer-matrix cliques
open: Determine the largest family of \(d\times d\) integer matrices whose pairwise differences have determinant \(\pm1\), or close its asymptotic upper–lower gap.
status: The 2026 work constructs size \(d^2\) for infinitely many \(d\) and resolves several small dimensions; general optimal sizes remain unknown.
why: Larger families improve algebraic challenge spaces for hidden-order-group proofs and black-box sharing.
key_works: Milan Boutros, Ignacio Cascudo, Ronald Cramer, Daniël van Gent and Chaoping Xing (2026), [*On Exceptional Cliques in Matrix Rings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24586).
aliases: Exceptional sets; subtractive sets; admissible sets in related formulations.

title: R3-012. Optimal linear sharing for low-density upslices
open: For fixed \(0<\alpha<1/2\), realize every monotone DNF with minterms of size \(\lceil\alpha n\rceil\) by linear sharing over \(\mathbb F_2\) with total length \(2^{H_2(\alpha)n/2+o(n)}\), or prove a larger exponent necessary; \(H_2\) is binary entropy.
status: Nir’s September 2026 preprint bounds the exponent analytically between \(H_2(\alpha)/2\) and \(H_2(\alpha)/(1+H_2(\alpha))\); numerical improvements leave the gap open.
why: Optimal low upslices would lower the unrestricted exponent below \(0.491\).
key_works: Oded Nir (2026), [*Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/146/revision/1/download), §1.3 and Corollaries 1.3–1.4.

title: R3-013. The quadratic secret-sharing exponent
open: Determine the worst-case share-size exponent for perfect one-bit secret sharing with sharing and reconstruction computed by degree-at-most-two polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\).
status: September 2026 bounds leave the exponent between \(1/3\) and \(0.4994\); quadratic sharing now strictly improves on linear sharing.
why: Measures the savings from one extra algebraic degree.
key_works: Oded Nir (2026), [*Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/146/revision/1/download), Theorem 1.6.

title: R3-014. Micciancio’s full-composability-to-circular-security conjecture
open: Does fully composable homomorphic encryption imply circular-secure encryption? Full composability requires evaluation and decryption to commute on every ciphertext; the derived scheme may differ.
status: Micciancio’s 2025 Conjecture 1. Bootstrapping supplies a converse under suitable homomorphism.
why: Would derive security from a stronger correctness requirement.
key_works: Daniele Micciancio (2025), [*Fully Composable Homomorphic Encryption*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/1/1), DOI:10.62056/ak5wl86bm, Conjecture 1.

title: R3-015. Safe two-scheme key cycles
open: For every public-key encryption scheme \(\mathrm{Enc}\), does some scheme \(\mathrm{Enc}'\) preserve \(\mathrm{Enc}\)’s security when \(\mathrm{Enc}'(sk)\) and \(\mathrm{Enc}(sk')\) are published, using independent keys?
status: Micciancio’s 2025 Conjecture 2; same-scheme cycle counterexamples do not settle it.
why: Would justify heterogeneous key cycles used in composability transformations.
key_works: Daniele Micciancio (2025), [*Fully Composable Homomorphic Encryption*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/1/1), DOI:10.62056/ak5wl86bm, Conjecture 2.

title: R3-016. Full composability from ordinary FHE alone
open: Does ordinary fully homomorphic encryption imply fully composable homomorphic encryption without a circular-security hypothesis?
status: Explicitly unresolved in Micciancio (2025); fresh-ciphertext correctness is insufficient.
why: Would close a gap between foundational FHE definitions and arbitrary composition.
key_works: Daniele Micciancio (2025), [*Fully Composable Homomorphic Encryption*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/1/1), DOI:10.62056/ak5wl86bm.

title: R3-017. Unbounded-circuit KDM security from ordinary LWE
open: Construct public-key encryption from ordinary LWE secure for every polynomial-size key-dependent-message circuit, with the scheme fixed independently of the circuit-size bound and number of keys. Permit adaptive circuit choices.
status: The distinction dates to 2010. Kitagawa–Matsuda’s 2020 amplification supports arbitrary numbers of keys but still requires an a priori circuit-size bound; circular-secure, circuit-private FHE gives the unbounded form under additional assumptions.
why: Would remove a predetermined complexity ceiling from applications encrypting key-dependent data.
key_works: Boaz Barak, Iftach Haitner, Dennis Hofheinz and Yuval Ishai (2010), [*Bounded Key-Dependent Message Security*](https://iftachh.github.io/MyHomepage/papers/BoundedKDM/boundedkdm.pdf); Fuyuki Kitagawa and Takahiro Matsuda (2020), [*Circular Security Is Complete for KDM Security*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/1060); Benny Applebaum (2014), [*Key-Dependent Message Security: Generic Amplification and Completeness*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-013-9149-6).

title: R3-018. Collision resistance at algebraic degree two
open: Construct a shrinking collision-resistant hash family whose coordinates are degree-two polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\), or prove that every efficiently sampled family admits efficient collision finding. A specially chosen hard distribution of quadratic maps is allowed.
status: Explicitly open since 2017. Degree three is achievable under codeword-hardness assumptions; random quadratic maps provide universal one-way hashing under a quadratic-system assumption but are not collision resistant.
why: Determines whether a single multiplication layer can support collision resistance.
key_works: Benny Applebaum, Naama Haramaty-Krasne, Yuval Ishai, Eyal Kushilevitz and Vinod Vaikuntanathan (2017), [*Low-Complexity Cryptographic Hash Functions*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.7).

title: R3-019. Almost-universal hashing with leading constant two and subexponential error
open: Construct almost-universal hashing on \(n\)-bit inputs with collision probability \(\exp(-n^{\Omega(1)})\), output length \(o(n)\), and \(2n+o(n)\) gates over \(B_2\), the basis of all two-input Boolean functions.
status: Fan–Li–Yang’s 2022 partial result uses \(3n\) gates nonuniformly. Chen–Li–Yang improve uniformity and seed length at \(2n+o(n)\), but their error is \(\exp(-\Omega(\log^2 n/\log\log n))\).
why: Would preserve stronger PRF security while reducing evaluation cost to its optimal leading constant.
key_works: Zhiyuan Fan, Jiatu Li and Tianqi Yang (2022), [*The Exact Complexity of Pseudorandom Functions and the Black-Box Natural Proof Barrier for Bootstrapping Results in Computational Complexity*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2021/125/revision/1/download), DOI:10.1145/3519935.3520010; Lijie Chen, Jiatu Li and Tianqi Yang (2022), [*Extremely Efficient Constructions of Hash Functions, with Applications to Hardness Magnification and PRFs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2022.23).

title: R3-020. Key homomorphism together with collusion-resistant constraint privacy
open: Obtain compute-and-compare constrained PRFs simultaneously supporting key homomorphism and collusion-resistant constraint privacy under standard LWE. Protect hidden constraints against coalitions holding multiple constrained keys.
status: Cheng–Goyal (2026) explicitly leave the simultaneous guarantee open.
why: Would allow algebraic manipulation of delegated keys without exposing protected constraints.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng and Rishab Goyal (2026), [*Collusion-Resistant Constrained PRFs for Compute-&-Compare Predicates from LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1874).

title: R3-021. Adaptive compute-and-compare CPRFs in the standard model
open: Prove adaptive security for collusion-resistant compute-and-compare constrained PRFs from ordinary LWE in the standard model, permitting relevant predicates to depend on previously obtained keys and outputs.
status: Cheng–Goyal (2026) establish selective security in the standard model and discuss adaptive security in the random-oracle model; eliminating the gap remains unresolved.
why: Removes advance commitment from fine-grained pseudorandom delegation.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng and Rishab Goyal (2026), [*Collusion-Resistant Constrained PRFs for Compute-&-Compare Predicates from LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1874).

title: R3-022. Collusion-resistant private puncturing from DCR
open: Extend privately constrained PRFs based on decisional composite residuosity to polynomially many colluding constrained keys, hiding punctured points under a multi-key privacy definition. Retain an exponentially large domain without stronger obfuscation or FHE assumptions.
status: Proposed extension of a 2025 frontier: Behera–Meyer–Orlandi–Roy–Scholl achieve single-key selective security for polynomially bounded Waring-rank predicates, including puncturing.
why: Enables multiple independent delegations using one algebraic PRF family.
key_works: Amik Raj Behera, Pierre Meyer, Claudio Orlandi, Lawrence Roy and Peter Scholl (2025), [*Privately Constrained PRFs from DCR: Puncturing and Bounded Waring Rank*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/230).

title: R3-023. Remove one input-dimension factor from registered quadratic FE setup
open: Reduce the CRS size of registered quadratic functional encryption from \(O(n^2L^2\log L)\) to \(O(nL^2\log L)\), for input dimension \(n\) and \(L\) registration slots, retaining compact ciphertexts and security.
status: Explicitly posed in 2024; ciphertexts already have size \(O(n+\log L)\).
why: Would remove a quadratic data-dimension cost from public setup.
key_works: Ziqi Zhu, Jiangtao Li, Kai Zhang, Junqing Gong and Haifeng Qian (2024), [*Registered Functional Encryptions from Pairings*](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-031-58723-8_13), DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-58723-8_13.

title: R3-024. Adaptive registered attribute-weighted sums with unbounded inputs
open: Construct registered FE for attribute-weighted sums with access control and an a priori unbounded number of attribute-value pairs, allowing adaptive challenge attributes, registrations and corruptions. Retain ciphertext compactness independent of public-input length under standard pairing assumptions.
status: Pal–Schädlich (2026) achieve adaptive IND security for one input pair. Their unbounded-input construction requires challenge attributes, registered functions and corrupted users to be declared upfront; closing that gap is the proposed target.
why: Supports changing encrypted records without advance knowledge of future access patterns.
key_works: Tapas Pal and Robert Schädlich (2026), [*Compact Registered Functional Encryption for Attribute-Weighted Sums with Access Control*](https://publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu/1000194419), DOI:10.1007/978-3-032-26737-5_11.

title: R3-025. The expressive power of pre-constrained registration
open: Characterize when pre-constrained registered inner-product FE realizes ordinary pre-constrained encryption, and when a converse compiler exists. Preserve the restriction that slot \(i\) registers functions only of the form \(M_i f_i\), for CRS-fixed \(M_i\), against malicious registration.
status: Zhu–Li–Zhang–Gong–Qian (2024) explicitly ask to clarify the relationship and develop general definitions and constructions beyond their specialized tool.
why: Identifies restrictions enforceable during registration independently of encrypted functionality.
key_works: Ziqi Zhu, Jiangtao Li, Kai Zhang, Junqing Gong and Haifeng Qian (2024), [*Registered Functional Encryptions from Pairings*](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-031-58723-8_13).

title: R3-026. Dishonest-registration lattice NIKE at polynomial noise ratio
open: Obtain dishonest-key-registration security for lattice-based noninteractive key exchange when the modulus-to-noise ratio is polynomial. Permit malformed and maliciously correlated registered public keys.
status: Langrehr–Tran (2026) explicitly pose this question. Their optimal linear-in-users reduction loss includes a polynomial-ratio regime with inverse-polynomial correctness error, but does not supply dishonest-registration security there.
why: Closes a security-model gap when public keys come from untrusted users.
key_works: Roman Langrehr and Si An Oliver Tran (2026), [*Lattice-based NIKE with optimal tightness*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1845).

title: R3-027. Non-black-box time-lock puzzles from VDFs alone
open: Construct time-lock puzzles from arbitrary ordinary verifiable delay functions using non-black-box techniques and no additional cryptographic assumption, or prove a stronger impossibility. Preserve fast puzzle generation and security against parallel solvers.
status: EUROCRYPT 2026 rules out fully black-box constructions in both directions and explicitly leaves non-black-box constructions open. Renawi’s 2020 thesis uses additional witness-encryption assumptions.
why: Determines whether publicly verifiable sequential work inherently supports encryption to the future.
key_works: Hamza Abusalah, Nivesh Aggarwal, Karen Azari, Chethan Kamath and Maximilian von Consbruch (2026), [*Separating Verifiable Delay Functions and Time-Lock Puzzles*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-25330-9_2); Omar Renawi (2020; repository deposit 2025), [*Time-Lock Puzzles from Verifiable Delay Functions and Witness Encryption*](https://publications.cispa.de/articles/thesis/Time-Lock_Puzzles_from_Verifiable_Delay_Functions_and_Witness_Encryption/30866072).

title: R3-028. Preprocessing-secure VDFs from arbitrary time-lock puzzles
open: Extend generic time-lock-puzzle-to-VDF constructions to adversaries that preprocess public parameters before receiving a challenge. Preserve succinct public verification without assumptions tailored to one algebraic VDF candidate.
status: Abusalah–Azari–Fiore–Kamath–Tairi obtain one-time VDFs from TLPs, iO and OWFs, with perfect soundness and \(O(\lambda)\)-bit proofs, but exclude preprocessing. The 2026 fully black-box separation permits upgrades using iO or non-black-box methods.
why: Would support durable public VDF parameters.
key_works: Hamza Abusalah, Karen Azari, Dario Fiore, Chethan Kamath and Erkan Tairi (2025; PKC 2026), [*On Verifiable Delay Functions from Time-Lock Puzzles*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1782); Abusalah et al. (2026), [*Separating Verifiable Delay Functions and Time-Lock Puzzles*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-25330-9_2).

title: R3-029. Standard-model proofs of persistent space from cryptographic assumptions alone
open: Construct nontrivial proofs of persistent space from CRH alone, or an ordinary assumption such as LWE, removing the separate exponential nondeterministic-circuit hardness assumption. Keep verification substantially cheaper than storing or reconstructing the claimed space.
status: Proposed assumption-reduction target following Ball–Guan (2026): their standard-model framework combines CRH with hardness of E for exponential-size nondeterministic circuits; nearly optimal parameters additionally use SNARGs for P.
why: Would base persistent-storage enforcement directly on ordinary cryptographic assumptions.
key_works: Marshall Ball and Jiaxin Guan (2026), [*A Complexity-Theoretic Approach to Proofs of Space*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1470), arXiv:2608.08993.

title: R3-030. Construct Strong Off-the-Record Deniability
open: Construct an interactive encryption protocol satisfying Strong Off-the-Record Deniability: both parties can answer coercion arriving during execution with mutually consistent fake claims.
status: Abapour (2026) defines SORD and explicitly leaves construction open. The paper’s threshold fully deniable encryption addresses post-execution deniability.
why: Would make deniability survive coercion while a conversation is ongoing.
key_works: Navid Abapour (2026), [*Threshold Fully Deniable Interactive Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1900), SSS 2026.

title: R3-031. Separate strong and ordinary off-the-record deniability
open: Prove a formal separation between ordinary off-the-record deniability and SORD, or establish a compiler showing equivalence under specified assumptions. The distinction must involve adaptive mid-execution coercion and consistency across fake claims.
status: Explicitly left open alongside SORD construction in 2026; introducing the definition does not establish a separation.
why: Determines whether existing deniability guarantees fundamentally miss a stronger coercion threat.
key_works: Navid Abapour (2026), [*Threshold Fully Deniable Interactive Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1900).

title: R3-032. Adaptive deletion for arbitrary monotone access structures
open: Construct information-theoretic secret sharing with adaptive certified deletion for every efficiently representable monotone access structure. The adversary may corrupt and delete shares sequentially, while its currently undeleted shares remain unauthorized.
status: Explicit since Bartusek–Raizes (2024). Threshold structures are achieved; their general-access construction has no-signaling security. Katz–Sela (2025) reiterate the privately verifiable information-theoretic question.
why: Supports deletion policies based on complex organizational authorization rules.
key_works: James Bartusek and Justin Raizes (2024), [*Secret Sharing with Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08117); Jonathan Katz and Ben Sela (2025), [*Secret Sharing with Publicly Verifiable Deletion*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1596), [EUROCRYPT slides](https://iacr.org/submit/files/slides/2025/eurocrypt/eurocrypt2025/234/234_slides.pdf).

title: R3-033. A joint adaptive and no-signaling deletion model
open: Define and realize a nontrivial deletion notion incorporating adaptive share corruption and distributed adversarial coalitions in one experiment. Specify communication and deletion schedules so that the notion strictly captures both existing threat models.
status: Posed in 2024. Bazin–Nishimaki prove that adaptive security does not imply no-signaling security; separate proofs of the two existing games do not provide the requested unification.
why: Distributed compromises can combine changes over time with isolation between attackers.
key_works: Bartusek–Raizes (2024), [*Secret Sharing with Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08117); Dominique Bazin and Ryo Nishimaki (2024), [*A Note on Security Definitions for Secret Sharing with Certified Deletion*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1690); Justin Raizes (2025), [*Quantum Approaches to Verifiable Deletion*](https://csd.cmu.edu/sites/default/files/phd-thesis/CMU-CS-25-107.pdf), §11.4.

title: R3-034. Threshold signing keys with certified deletion
open: Construct threshold signatures whose quantum signing-key shares can be certifiably deleted, preserving unforgeability against sequential compromises whenever too few undeleted shares have accumulated. Authorized parties must still produce independently combinable partial signatures.
status: Explicitly posed in 2024 and Raizes’s 2025 thesis. Deletion of threshold secret shares does not itself provide reusable signing on protected shares.
why: Makes retirement of distributed signing authority cryptographically checkable.
key_works: Bartusek–Raizes (2024), [*Secret Sharing with Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08117); Justin Raizes (2025), [*Quantum Approaches to Verifiable Deletion*](https://csd.cmu.edu/sites/default/files/phd-thesis/CMU-CS-25-107.pdf), §11.4; Yvo Desmedt and Yair Frankel (1989/1990), [*Threshold Cryptosystems*](https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-34805-0_28).

title: R3-035. Information-theoretic publicly verifiable share deletion
open: Build secret sharing whose deletion certificates anyone can verify, with information-theoretic security and no computational hardness assumption. Verification must not require cooperation from every remaining shareholder.
status: Explicitly open in Chen–Ji–Luo (2026). Katz–Sela obtain computational public verification; Chen–Ji–Luo obtain information-theoretic, adaptive, linearly homomorphic threshold sharing with unanimous verification.
why: Permits public audits of distributed erasure without permanent hardness assumptions.
key_works: Jonathan Katz and Ben Sela (2025), [*Secret Sharing with Publicly Verifiable Deletion*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1596); Yilei Chen, Liheng Ji and Han Luo (2026), [*Linearly Homomorphic Secret Sharing and Multi-Party Computation with Unanimously Verifiable Deletion*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1673).

title: R3-036. Public deletion verification for CE-NIZK without iO
open: Obtain statistically sound NP NIZK with publicly verifiable deletion and certified-everlasting zero knowledge without assuming indistinguishability obfuscation.
status: Explicit in Pappu’s September 2026 revision; LWE constructions provide private verification, while a coset-state/iO route is suggested.
why: Supports independent deletion audits.
key_works: Nikhil Pappu (2025; revised 2026), [*Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13628v4), §2.7.

title: R3-037. Classical deletion certificates for CE-NIZK in the CRS model
open: Replace quantum-state return with a classical deletion certificate in CRS-model certified-everlasting NP NIZK, retaining statistical soundness.
status: Explicit in September 2026; the CRS construction requires quantum revocation. The shared-EPR alternative does not resolve this setup-specific target.
why: Enables classical certificate transport.
key_works: Nikhil Pappu (2025; revised 2026), [*Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13628v4), §2.7.

title: R3-038. Plain-model certified-everlasting NIWI
open: Construct plain-model, statistically sound noninteractive witness-indistinguishable proofs with computational WI before deletion and statistical WI after accepted deletion.
status: Explicit in September 2026; replacing the CE-NIZK construction’s outer ZK proofs by WI proofs defeats its current simulation argument.
why: Removes shared setup.
key_works: Nikhil Pappu (2025; revised 2026), [*Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13628v4), §2.7.

title: R3-039. Certified-everlasting NIZK for QMA with quantum setup
open: Extend certified-everlasting NIZK to QMA using designated-verifier or shared-EPR setup, including statistical soundness and post-deletion witness privacy.
status: Explicit in September 2026; interactive CE-ZK covers QMA, whereas this CE-NIZK construction covers NP.
why: Protects consumed quantum witnesses.
key_works: Nikhil Pappu (2025; revised 2026), [*Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13628v4); Taiga Hiroka, Tomoyuki Morimae, Ryo Nishimaki and Takashi Yamakawa (2022), [*Certified Everlasting Zero-Knowledge Proof for QMA*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-15802-5_9).

title: R3-040. Near-unit quantum rate for deletion with authorized leakage
open: Proposed quantitative target: raise the quantum communication rate of coset-based certified deletion from \(1/4\) toward \(1-\varepsilon\), for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), while preserving the underlying primitive’s permitted functional leakage.
status: Chung–Huang–Hung–Yamada’s October 2026 preprint achieves \(1/4\) for coset-based applications; its BB84 compiler reaches \(1-\varepsilon\) for long messages.
why: Smaller quantum payloads make deletion-compatible FE and leased computation less demanding.
key_works: Kai-Min Chung, Tzu-Hsiang Huang, Wei-Hsiang Hung and Shota Yamada (2026), [*Constant-Rate Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.03590v1), §§1.1–2.

title: R3-041. Constant-rate publicly verifiable deletion from OWFs
open: Proposed assumption target: construct constant-quantum-rate publicly verifiable deletion for commitments or secret-key encryption from arbitrary post-quantum one-way functions.
status: The October 2026 constant-rate public compiler uses SIS; earlier OWF-based public-verification techniques lose rate. Constant-rate private deletion is achieved.
why: Retains communication efficiency at the minimal classical assumption level.
key_works: Chung, Huang, Hung and Yamada (2026), [*Constant-Rate Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.03590v1), §7; Fuyuki Kitagawa, Ryo Nishimaki and Takashi Yamakawa (2023), [*Publicly Verifiable Deletion from Minimal Assumptions*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-48624-1_9).

title: R3-042. Standard-model decisional proofs of no intrusion
open: Construct reusable, nondestructive proofs of no intrusion for a classical client under LWE in the standard model, with everlasting indistinguishability of plaintext bits in an outside attacker’s residual state.
status: Goyal–Raizes pose decisional security. Kalai–Raizes’s September 2026 preprint achieves classical upload and everlasting search security from LWE, but its decisional construction uses the QROM.
why: An accepted audit would certify absence of partial-message leakage while preserving stored data.
key_works: Vipul Goyal and Justin Raizes (2025; EUROCRYPT 2026), [*Proofs of No Intrusion*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06432v1), §2.4; Yael Tauman Kalai and Justin Raizes (2026), [*Semi-Quantum Cryptography with Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.38915v1).

title: R3-043. Plain-model certified-deniable signatures beyond black-box simulation
open: Construct plain-model signatures with certified deniability using a non-black-box simulator, or extend the impossibility to such simulators. After deletion, retained evidence must be simulatable without the signature beyond independently available prior information.
status: Çakan–Goyal–Raizes give QROM constructions and a plain-model black-box simulation barrier; the stronger impossibility is not established.
why: Determines whether a verifier can credibly erase evidence of a signed interaction without an idealized oracle.
key_works: Alper Çakan, Vipul Goyal and Justin Raizes (2024; revised 2025; CRYPTO 2026), [*How to Delete Without a Trace: Certified Deniability in a Quantum World*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1832); Justin Raizes (2025), [*Quantum Approaches to Verifiable Deletion*](https://csd.cmu.edu/sites/default/files/phd-thesis/CMU-CS-25-107.pdf), Part III.

title: R3-044. Plain-model stateful quantum iO
open: Construct plain-model quantum iO taking an evaluator and an unknown, evolving private quantum state, with equivalence defined over all adaptive sequences of forward and inverse evaluations.
status: Explicit in the October 2026 revision; ideal-unitary-obfuscation and classical-oracle constructions are known. The target uses stateful sequential equivalence, distinct from earlier channel and pseudo-deterministic-program interfaces.
why: Supports evolving quantum secrets.
key_works: Aparna Gupte, Jiahui Liu, Luowen Qian, Justin Raizes, Bhaskar Roberts and Mark Zhandry (2026), [*On Best-Possible One-Time Programs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00544v2), §1.9.

title: R3-045. Does unitary iO imply stateful quantum iO?
open: Derive stateful quantum iO from ordinary unitary iO, replacing the known ideal-obfuscation assumption.
status: Explicit in October 2026; the unresolved step is protecting the authentication key hiding the evolving state register.
why: Connects two obfuscation models.
key_works: Gupte, Liu, Qian, Raizes, Roberts and Zhandry (2026), [*On Best-Possible One-Time Programs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00544v2), §1.9.

title: R3-046. Plain-model best-possible testable one-time programs
open: Construct plain-model one-time compilers whose leakage is minimal among implementations supplied with a reflection test for their program state, for arbitrary quantum functionalities.
status: Explicit in October 2026; stateful iO would suffice, and oracle constructions exist.
why: Clarifies attainable one-time privacy.
key_works: Gupte, Liu, Qian, Raizes, Roberts and Zhandry (2026), [*On Best-Possible One-Time Programs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00544v2), §1.9.

title: R3-047. Simultaneous-message QKD with full everlasting security
open: Obtain QKD with two simultaneous messages and standard everlasting security, including agreement-or-abort under active attacks.
status: Explicit in 2025; known simultaneous-message security is a conditional search guarantee. Four messages over two rounds achieve full security.
why: Enables independent sending.
key_works: Alex B. Grilo, Giulio Malavolta, Michael Walter and Tianwei Zhang (2025; proceedings 2026), [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3.

title: R3-048. Positive key rate in two-round EPR-based QKD
open: Achieve standard everlasting security and \(\Omega(n)\) secret key bits from \(n\) transmitted qubits in two rounds, using EPR pairs and single-qubit measurements.
status: The 2025 computational-monogamy protocol achieves two rounds; positive key rate is explicitly left open.
why: Improves usable key yield.
key_works: Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang (2025; proceedings 2026), [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3.

title: R3-049. Computational monogamy with arbitrary efficient Bob measurements
open: In computational monogamy with an initially computationally hidden BB84 basis, allow Bob any efficient basis-dependent POVM while Charlie remains unbounded; bound their joint guessing probability negligibly.
status: Explicit in 2025; the theorem requires Bob’s prescribed basis measurement.
why: Handles adversarial recipient processing.
key_works: Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang (2025), [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3.

title: R3-050. Computational monogamy with two unbounded measurement stages
open: Strengthen the same game to arbitrary unbounded POVMs for both Bob and Charlie after efficient state preparation with a computationally hidden basis.
status: Explicit in 2025; even allowing only efficient arbitrary Bob measurements remains unresolved.
why: Separates preparation and measurement complexity.
key_works: Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang (2025), [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3.

title: R3-051. Two-message QKD in the qubit-by-qubit model
open: Construct two-message everlasting-secure QKD whose states and operations follow the qubit-by-qubit model, without coherent joint processing of polynomial-size quantum registers.
status: Malavolta–Walter explicitly pose this restriction in 2023/2024; their OWF-based two-message construction uses many-qubit superpositions.
why: Makes minimal interaction compatible with simpler quantum optical hardware.
key_works: Giulio Malavolta and Michael Walter (2023; revised 2024), [*Robust Quantum Public-Key Encryption with Applications to Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.02999), §1.3.

title: R3-052. Noise-efficient two-message everlasting QKD
open: Design and analyze two-message everlasting-secure QKD with efficient handling of a specified nonzero noise rate, including concrete finite-size secrecy and correctness bounds.
status: Explicit since 2023/2024. Generic quantum error correction provides a theoretical route, but concrete noise efficiency remains unresolved.
why: A round-optimal protocol needs a workable error-correction and reconciliation budget.
key_works: Giulio Malavolta and Michael Walter (2023; revised 2024), [*Robust Quantum Public-Key Encryption with Applications to Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.02999), §1.3.

title: R3-053. A natural complete problem for instance hiding
open: Find a natural complete problem, under an explicitly specified efficient reduction, for languages admitting statistically instance-hiding interactive proofs.
status: Explicitly open in Mu–Vasudevan’s 2026 journal version; closure properties do not supply such a problem.
why: Gives private delegation a canonical reduction target.
key_works: Changrui Mu and Prashant Nalini Vasudevan (2024; journal 2026), [*Instance-Hiding Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09573-w), §1.4.

title: R3-054. The reverse SZK–instance-hiding oracle separation
open: Construct an oracle \(O\) with \(\mathrm{SZK}^O\not\subseteq\mathrm{IHIP}^O\), or prove the corresponding containment.
status: Mu–Vasudevan establish an oracle with \(\mathrm{IHIP}^O\not\subseteq\mathrm{SZK}^O\); the reverse direction remains open.
why: Distinguishes hiding a verifier’s instance from hiding a prover’s witness.
key_works: Changrui Mu and Prashant Nalini Vasudevan (2024; journal 2026), [*Instance-Hiding Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09573-w).

title: R3-055. Complement closure with a simulatable prover
open: Prove or refute that Simulatable-IHIP is closed under complement.
status: Ordinary IHIP has complement closure; its simulatable variant remains open in 2026.
why: Determines whether privately proving rejection is as feasible as proving acceptance.
key_works: Changrui Mu and Prashant Nalini Vasudevan (2024; journal 2026), [*Instance-Hiding Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09573-w), §1.4, Question 3.
aliases: Strong-IHIP complement closure in the earlier terminology.

title: R3-056. Amplification of instance-hiding privacy
open: Reduce instance-hiding statistical error to negligible error through an efficient generic transformation preserving completeness and soundness.
status: Explicitly open in the 2026 journal treatment. September 2026 amplification for one-sided randomized encodings does not settle this interactive, input-independent simulation requirement.
why: Permits protocols to start from weaker privacy guarantees.
key_works: Mu–Vasudevan (2026), [*Instance-Hiding Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09573-w), Question 6; Pouria Fallahpour, Alex B. Grilo, Garazi Muguruza and Mahshid Riahinia (2025; revised 2026), [*Amplifying Randomized Encodings & Applications*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21442), v3.

title: R3-057. Statistical randomized encodings of degree two
open: Decide whether every finite Boolean function has a statistical randomized encoding whose output coordinates are degree-at-most-two polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\) in input and random bits.
status: Degree three suffices; perfect-privacy lower bounds do not settle the statistical relaxation. This boundary is explicitly identified in the literature.
why: Would lower the algebraic complexity of information-theoretic secure computation.
key_works: Benny Applebaum (2017), [*Garbled Circuits as Randomized Encodings of Functions: A Primer*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2017/067/), §4.1; Shai Halevi, Yuval Ishai, Eyal Kushilevitz and Tal Rabin (2023), [*Additive Randomized Encodings and Their Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/870).

title: R3-058. Statistical randomized encodings of locality three
open: Decide whether every finite Boolean function admits a statistically private encoding in which each output bit depends on at most three input-or-randomness bits.
status: Locality four is achievable; locality two is insufficient in general. The intermediate statistical case remains unresolved in the cited treatment.
why: Measures the smallest local operation supporting general private encodings.
key_works: Benny Applebaum (2017), [*Garbled Circuits as Randomized Encodings of Functions: A Primer*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2017/067/), §4.1.

title: R3-059. Perfectly correct statistical additive encodings
open: Construct statistically private additive randomized encodings for every finite multiparty function with perfect correctness: decoding must always return the true output without a failure symbol.
status: The STOC 2026 universality theorem allows statistical correctness error and explicitly leaves perfect correctness open. Computational perfect correctness does not establish this information-theoretic target.
why: Removes errors and aborts from anonymous computation based on summing encodings.
key_works: Nir Bitansky, Saroja Erabelli, Rachit Garg and Yuval Ishai (2026), [*Shuffling Is Universal: Statistical Additive Randomized Encodings for All Functions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1442), DOI:10.1145/3798129.3800890.

title: R3-060. Statistical robust additive encodings for finite functions
open: For every fixed finite multiparty function \(f\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), construct a robust additive randomized encoding with statistical correctness and privacy errors at most \(\varepsilon\), revealing only the residual function determined by honest inputs. Allow unrestricted dependence of encoding size on \(f\).
status: The STOC 2026 universality paper explicitly leaves finite-function robustness open. September robust constructions use computational assumptions and do not settle it.
why: Could bridge anonymous computation and information-theoretic MPC against larger coalitions.
key_works: Halevi, Ishai, Kushilevitz and Rabin (2023), [*Additive Randomized Encodings and Their Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/870); Bitansky, Erabelli, Garg and Ishai (2026), [*Shuffling Is Universal*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1442); Sapir Bekerman Freizeit and Nir Bitansky (2026), [*Robust Additive Randomized Encodings With Transparent Setup*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1937).

title: R3-061. One-round framing-free distributed ZK
open: In the ideal-coin-tossing model, obtain a one-round information-theoretic distributed ZK proof with strong completeness against malicious verifiers, or prove two rounds necessary. Retain verification communication independent of statement circuit size.
status: Hazay–Venkitasubramaniam–Weiss obtain two rounds for appropriately robustly encoded statements and \(k>6t+2\); they explicitly leave round optimality open.
why: Makes private input certification compatible with one upload followed by verification.
key_works: Carmit Hazay, Muthuramakrishnan Venkitasubramaniam and Mor Weiss (2023; journal 2026), [*Your Reputation’s Safe with Me: Framing-Free Distributed Zero-Knowledge Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09576-7), §1.3.

title: R3-062. Sublinear framing-free proofs for low-degree relations
open: Construct special-purpose strongly complete distributed ZK proofs for low-degree NP relations with sublinear total proof communication and efficient verification, retaining information-theoretic security against malicious verifiers.
status: The general construction is quasilinear in circuit size in two rounds, or linear in three; specialized sublinear constructions are explicitly left open.
why: Makes maliciously secure aggregation and input validation less communication-intensive.
key_works: Hazay, Venkitasubramaniam and Weiss (2023; journal 2026), [*Your Reputation’s Safe with Me: Framing-Free Distributed Zero-Knowledge Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09576-7), §1.3.

title: R3-063. Polynomial-loss reduction from local sources to local NOBF sources
open: Reduce every \(d\)-local source of min-entropy \(k\) to a distribution exponentially close to a mixture of \(d\)-local nonoblivious bit-fixing sources retaining \(\Omega(k/\operatorname{poly}(d))\) entropy, or prove this impossible. Each original output bit depends on at most \(d\) uniform input bits.
status: Explicitly posed in 2022. The known reduction retains \(\Omega(k/(2^d d^2))\) entropy.
why: Extends local-source extraction to growing locality.
key_works: Omar Alrabiah, Eshan Chattopadhyay, Jesse Goodman, Xin Li and João Ribeiro (2022), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Extract from Local Sources*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13725), Theorem 2 and §1.2; DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2022.10.

title: R3-064. Sharp low-weight Chevalley–Warning bounds for quadratic systems
open: Determine the sharp \(n,m\)-dependent upper bound on the minimum Hamming weight of a nonzero common zero of \(m\) quadratic polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\), assuming all vanish at zero and \(2m<n\). Can a linear-in-\(m\) bound remain necessary when \(n/m\) grows?
status: The 2022 low-weight Chevalley–Warning theorem gives \(O(m)\); tightness for quadratic systems remains explicitly unresolved.
why: Controls algebraic obstructions to extraction and sparse polynomial-system solutions.
key_works: Alrabiah, Chattopadhyay, Goodman, Li and Ribeiro (2022), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Extract from Local Sources*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13725), Theorem 4 and §1.2.

title: R3-065. Existential degree threshold for sumset dispersers
open: Determine the minimum entropy at which a degree-\(d\) polynomial over \(\mathbb F_2\) disperses every sumset source \(A+B\), where \(A,B\) are independent and each has min-entropy at least \(k\). Establish the existence threshold with matching impossibility bounds.
status: The 2025 bounds leave sufficiency at \(k=O(dn^{1/\lfloor d/2\rfloor})\) versus impossibility at \(k=c d n^{1/(d-1)}\).
why: Identifies low-degree maps’ power before addressing explicit construction.
key_works: Omar Alrabiah, Jesse Goodman, Jonathan Mosheiff and João Ribeiro (2025), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Are Good Extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10297), §7; DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2025.38.

title: R3-066. Exponentially small error for random constant-degree sumset extractors
open: Prove the conjecture that most degree-\(d\) polynomials extract from sumset sources at entropy \(k=Cdn^{C/d}\) with exponentially small error, even for fixed \(d\). A concrete milestone is error \(2^{-n^{\Omega(1)}}\) at a small constant entropy rate.
status: Posed in 2025. For even \(d\), the current general bound requires \(k=O(d(n/\varepsilon^2)^{2/d})\), preventing this error regime at fixed degree.
why: Supplies strong statistical security without increasing algebraic degree with the error parameter.
key_works: Alrabiah, Goodman, Mosheiff and Ribeiro (2025), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Are Good Extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10297), Theorem 2 and §7.

title: R3-067. Explicit distributions resisting AC0-with-parity samplers
open: Construct an explicit polynomial-time samplable distribution on \(n\) bits whose total-variation distance from every polynomial-size, constant-depth \(\mathrm{AC}^0[\oplus]\) sampler is \(1-o(1)\), allowing arbitrarily many uniform input bits. Even a nontrivial constant separation is progress.
status: Explicitly open in July 2026. Strong bounds for ordinary \(\mathrm{AC}^0\) and bounded-degree polynomial maps do not establish this target.
why: Separates efficient distribution generation from shallow parallel generation.
key_works: Farzan Byramji, Daniel M. Kane, Jackson Morris and Anthony Ostuni (2026), [*Hard-to-Sample Distributions from Robust Extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26179), §5, Question 1.

title: R3-068. Repetition that amplifies isolator robustness
open: Strengthen the robust-extractor/isolator framework so its sampling-hardness error contribution \(\beta\) decreases with repetition count \(t\), under explicit source-closure and robustness hypotheses. Preserve useful bounds on the excluded sampler’s complexity.
status: Theorem 2.5 of the July 2026 paper leaves an additive \(\beta\) term unaffected by repetition; Question 3 asks for amplification, potentially through a stronger extraction object.
why: Produces sharper direct-product lower bounds for approximate sampling.
key_works: Byramji, Kane, Morris and Ostuni (2026), [*Hard-to-Sample Distributions from Robust Extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26179), Theorem 2.5 and §5.

title: R3-069. Breaking the logarithm-squared seed barrier at width four
open: Construct an explicit generator fooling every length-\(n\), width-four read-once branching program to fixed constant error with seed length \(o(\log^2 n)\). Impose no regularity, permutation or commutativity restriction.
status: Nisan’s 1992 bound remains unbroken for width four; the 2026 weighted-generator treatment identifies this smallest outstanding width. Width three admits improvements.
why: Tests whether small-space derandomization extends beyond specially structured transitions.
key_works: Ben Chen, Gil Cohen, Dean Doron, Yuval Khaskelberg and Amnon Ta-Shma (2026), [*Improved Error Reduction for Weighted PRGs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/064/), revision 3; Noam Nisan (1992), *Pseudorandom Generators for Space-Bounded Computation*.

title: R3-070. Additive width dependence in weighted pseudorandom generators
open: Construct a space-efficient weighted PRG for length-\(n\), width-\(w\) branching programs with seed length \(O(\log^2 n+\log(w/\varepsilon))\). Signed weights are allowed, with generation and evaluation satisfying the derandomization’s space requirements.
status: Hoza’s 2021 bound is \(O(\log n\log(nw)+\log(1/\varepsilon))\); 2026 work improves very large widths without achieving additive width dependence generally.
why: Would imply \(\mathrm{BPL}\subseteq\operatorname{DSPACE}(\log^{4/3}n)\).
key_works: Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma (2026), [*Improved Error Reduction for Weighted PRGs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/064/), revision 3, §1.

title: R3-071. Alphabet dependence of INW for permutation programs
open: Determine optimal alphabet-size dependence in the INW generator for permutation branching programs, tracking length, width and error. Close the gap between current logarithmic dependence on alphabet size \(d\) and the \(\Omega(\log n\log\log\min\{n,d\})\) obstruction to spectral analyses, or strengthen that obstruction.
status: The 2026 forward–backward analysis is optimal within the spectral framework for binary alphabets; larger alphabets remain explicitly open.
why: Avoids excessive cost for randomized transitions with many symbols.
key_works: Gil Cohen, Dean Doron and Noam Goldgraber (2026), [*A Forward-Backward Weight Analysis of INW for Permutation Branching Programs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/123/), §1.2.

title: R3-072. Optimal small-error generators for S3 products
open: Construct an explicit \(\varepsilon\)-error generator for read-once products over \(S_3\) with seed \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\). In particular, obtain logarithmic seed at inverse-polynomial error.
status: Lee–Viola (2025) attain the optimal bound for every fixed \(p\)-group but identify \(S_3\), of order six, as unresolved. The 2026 general permutation-program INW bound still multiplies \(\log n\) by \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\).
why: Isolates an obstruction from mixing prime factors in a small noncommutative group.
key_works: Chin Ho Lee and Emanuele Viola (2025), [*Pseudorandom Bits for Non-Commutative Programs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.9), §1.2; Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber (2026), [*A Forward-Backward Weight Analysis of INW for Permutation Branching Programs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/123/).
aliases: Optimal small-error PRGs for width-three permutation branching programs.

title: R3-073. Lifting group-product generators to arbitrary group-valued blocks
open: Extend the near-optimal group-product-to-block-product reduction to \(\prod_i h_i(x_{I_i})\), with arbitrary group-valued maps on disjoint blocks. Preserve near-optimal seed dependence on block width, block count and error for a fixed noncommutative mixing group such as the quaternions.
status: The 2025 reduction treats \(g_i^{f_i(x_{I_i})}\) with Boolean \(f_i\); extending the block’s range to the entire group is explicitly open.
why: Removes a Boolean-exponent restriction from algebraic derandomization.
key_works: Chin Ho Lee and Emanuele Viola (2025), [*Pseudorandom Bits for Non-Commutative Programs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.9), Theorem 10 and §1.2.

title: R3-074. Finite-file capacity of X-secure T-private retrieval
open: Determine exact download capacity for \(K\) files on \(N\) servers when any \(X\) stored server states reveal no file information and any \(T\) query transcripts reveal no requested index. Optimize the storage encoding and retain finite \(K\).
status: The 2018/2019 result determines asymptotic capacity \(1-(X+T)/N\) for \(N>X+T\), plus selected finite-\(K\) cases. The 2026 storage paper confirms even general finite-file \(T=1\) remains open.
why: Quantifies the combined cost of hiding stored data and requests.
key_works: Zhuqing Jia, Hua Sun and Syed Ali Jafar (2018/2019), [*Cross Subspace Alignment and the Asymptotic Capacity of X-Secure T-Private Information Retrieval*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07457); Mohamed Nomeir and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*Storage-Rate Trade-off in A-XPIR*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14202).

title: R3-075. Storage–download regions for asymmetric secure PIR
open: Characterize the achievable average-storage/average-download region when a specified hypergraph of server coalitions must learn no stored data, while individual servers learn no requested index. Allow arbitrary storage encodings and coalition patterns.
status: In 2026, the region is solved for four servers, two files and two disjoint communicating pairs. General counts have outer bounds and selected constructions without matching regions.
why: Makes private storage reflect actual trust relationships.
key_works: Mohamed Nomeir and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*Storage-Rate Trade-off in A-XPIR*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14202), June revision.

title: R3-076. Addition-only multi-message PIR when demand size does not divide file count
open: Determine the best download rate of addition-only linear PIR retrieving any \(D\)-subset of \(K\) replicated files from \(N\) noncolluding servers when \(D\nmid K\). Match achievability with a converse for this coefficient-restricted class.
status: The 2025 linear-programming construction improves previous rates but leaves gaps in the nondivisible regime. Both constructions and converse bounds may be improvable.
why: Determines whether inexpensive additions achieve optimal batch-retrieval rates.
key_works: Anoosheh Heidarzadeh, Ningze Wang and Alex Sprintson (2025), [*A Linear Programming Approach to Private Information Retrieval*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12286).

title: R3-077. Exact one-neighbor private retrieval on a path
open: Determine capacity on an \(N\)-server path, \(N\ge6\), with each message stored at its edge endpoints and each server hiding requests for messages held by itself or either immediate neighbor. Close
status: These bounds follow from the September 2026 two-sided-neighbor theorem at \(h=1\); exact capacity remains undetermined.
why: Quantifies the price of extending privacy one hop beyond a file’s storage locations.
key_works: Mohamed Nomeir, Shreya Meel and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*Private Information Retrieval With Arbitrary Privacy Requirements: Introduction and Capacity Results*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15875), Theorem 7.

title: R3-078. Joint rate–randomness–subpacketization region for structured subset retrieval
open: For a specified family of \(D\)-element demands, maximize secure retrieval rate under simultaneous shared-randomness and subpacketization budgets in balanced \(\{0,1\}\)-linear schemes. Hide the demand subset from each server and all unrequested files from the user.
status: May 2026 work solves the optimal-rate corner: \(1-1/N\), randomness ratio \(D/(N-1)\), and subpacketization \((N-1)/\gcd(D,N-1)\). The constrained region remains open.
why: Makes retrieval guarantees useful under independent packet and key-storage limits.
key_works: Maha Issa and Anoosheh Heidarzadeh (2026), [*Secure and Private Structured-Subset Retrieval: Fundamental Limits and Achievable Schemes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09368), §VII.

title: R3-079. Asymmetric subpacketization in secure structured-subset retrieval
open: Determine minimum subpacketization at rate \(1-1/N\) when fixed-length linear answers may have unequal lengths across servers. Can asymmetry beat the balanced bound \((N-1)/\gcd(D,N-1)\)?
status: Explicitly posed in May 2026. The proven minimum applies to balanced schemes and does not establish the asymmetric minimum.
why: Can reduce fragmentation without weakening request privacy or database secrecy.
key_works: Maha Issa and Anoosheh Heidarzadeh (2026), [*Secure and Private Structured-Subset Retrieval: Fundamental Limits and Achievable Schemes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09368), §VII.

title: R3-080. Leaky joint demand-and-side-information privacy beyond one known file
open: Characterize optimal download cost for \(\varepsilon\)-differentially private retrieval with \(M\ge2\) privately held side-information files, protecting both the desired index and side-information index set. Use \(N\) noncommunicating replicas of \(K\) files.
status: Huangfu–Bai’s January 2026 construction handles \(M=1\), recovering perfect-privacy limits as \(\varepsilon\to0\). General \(M\ge2\) costs and matching converses remain explicitly open.
why: Quantifies the value of private cached knowledge under controlled leakage.
key_works: Yingying Huangfu and Tian Bai (2026), [*On the Leaky Private Information Retrieval with Side Information*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09960), §5.

title: R3-081. Can graph-replicated secret randomness beat rate 1/N?
open: Does any connected storage graph on \(N\ge3\) servers permit symmetric PIR rate above \(1/N\) when each edge-message has independent secret randomness shared only by its endpoints? Retain the paper’s stronger database-privacy condition, including conditioning on other message-specific secrets.
status: In 2026, \(1/N\) is universally achievable and optimal for paths and regular graphs. A graph with higher capacity is explicitly unresolved.
why: Determines whether topology helps when masks cannot be shared globally.
key_works: Shreya Meel and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*The Role of Common Randomness Replication in Symmetric PIR on Graph-Based Replicated Systems*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16700), Theorems 1–3 and §7.

title: R3-082. Feasibility of SPIR with partially replicated common randomness
open: Given a message-placement graph and a separate hypergraph specifying which servers share each independent secret random variable, characterize positive-rate symmetric-PIR feasibility. Specify database privacy and determine minimum randomness budgets.
status: The 2026 study treats edge-local and global randomness and explicitly asks about intermediate replication. Its endpoint models use different database-privacy requirements, preventing an immediate general characterization.
why: Identifies sufficient key-distribution arrangements before bandwidth optimization.
key_works: Shreya Meel and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*The Role of Common Randomness Replication in Symmetric PIR on Graph-Based Replicated Systems*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16700), §7.

title: R3-083. The Grand MCA threshold at cryptographic error
open: For a Reed–Solomon code \(C\) on a smooth evaluation domain at rate \(1/2,1/4,1/8\), or \(1/16\), determine the largest proximity radius \(\delta^*\) satisfying \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mca}}(C,\delta^*)\le2^{-128}\), with explicit field-size dependence.
status: Formalized for the 2026 Proximity Prize. Jeronimo’s September preprint supplies fixed-slack asymptotic certificates over prime fields while leaving the largest safe radius and near-capacity window unresolved.
why: Sharp bounds reduce repetition and query costs in hash-based succinct proofs.
key_works: Gal Arnon, Dan Boneh and Giacomo Fenzi (2026), [*Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/680); Fernando Granha Jeronimo (2026), [*Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed–Solomon Codes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05870), preprint.
prize: Part of the Ethereum Foundation’s shared [**$1,000,000 Proximity Prize pool**](https://proximityprize.org/). Posted conditions are preliminary; the deadline is **31 December 2027**. Awards share the pool across challenges and qualifying results.

title: R3-084. The Grand interleaved list-decoding threshold
open: For the same rate/domain regime and fixed interleaving degree \(m\), find the largest \(\delta^*\) such that every radius-\(\delta^*\) ball in \(C^{\equiv m}\) contains at most \(2^{-128}|\mathbb F|\) codewords, measuring distance by disagreeing columns.
status: The challenge asks for the exact safe radius. The September prime-field preprint gives polynomial-size lists at every fixed positive slack below capacity without determining that optimum.
why: Converts list bounds into concrete algebraic-proof soundness guarantees.
key_works: Arnon, Boneh and Fenzi (2026), [*Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/680); Fernando Granha Jeronimo (2026), [*Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed–Solomon Codes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05870), §§8.2–8.5.
prize: Eligible contributions share the **same $1,000,000 pool** described in R3-083, subject to the [posted preliminary conditions](https://proximityprize.org/).

title: R3-085. Closing the Lean-verified koalaIRS12 soundness interval
open: Tighten, ideally close, the formally verified soundness interval for the companion challenge’s fixed **koalaIRS12** protocol by supplying a stronger proof or matching attack accepted by the Lean checker.
status: The live board checked on 9 October 2026 reports **68.15 proved security bits versus a 116.13-bit attack bound**, with **81 promoted submissions**. These concern this particular formalized protocol.
why: Gives a machine-checkable target where improvements directly change an auditable security estimate.
key_works: Yukon and zkSecurity (2026), [*The Proximity Prize companion challenge*](https://better.codes/); Arnon, Boneh and Fenzi (2026), [*Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/680), Construction 6.9.

title: R3-086. Up-front grants for the Proximity Prize questions
open: Proposed funding target: establish an openly administered program funding work on the two proximity challenges before a qualifying solution, including proof checking and unsuccessful but informative attacks.
status: The current prize FAQ explicitly says the program cannot award research grants; awards reward qualifying results. This is a documented program-level gap, without asserting an absence of outside funding.
why: Enables researchers without sufficient institutional support to pursue long, uncertain proof efforts.
key_works: Ethereum Foundation (2026), [*The Proximity Prize*](https://proximityprize.org/), grant FAQ and submission conditions.
